vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning

paras: The call lasted fifty minutes and there were nine people on it, from five countries. Everybody left it believing the same thing: that it had gone well, that the issue was understood, and that somebody would fix it. Six weeks later the same issue came back to the same nine people, and it took another fifty minutes to discover that nobody had ever agreed who somebody was.

Diana Okoro was the most junior person on that first call and she is the one who changed how the team works, although she says the change was accidental. She had taken notes because she was new and did not trust her memory, and the day after the call she sent them out. Not minutes — nobody reads minutes. A short recap: four lines about what had been decided, three action items with a name and a date on each, and one line at the bottom saying what was still pending and who it was waiting for.

The first reaction was silence, and then two corrections. One person wrote back to say that he had not agreed to deliver anything by the fifteenth, only to look at it. Another said the second decision had been the opposite of what Diana had written. Both corrections arrived within an hour. “That is the whole value,” she says now. “Not the summary. The corrections. Two people read four lines and discovered that the three of us had left that call with three different meetings in our heads.”

It is now a rule on her team, and it costs eight minutes. Whoever called the meeting writes the recap the same day, copies in anybody who was mentioned but not present, and closes with the single takeaway. The reason it works is not discipline. It is that a decision said out loud can hold two meanings comfortably, and a decision in writing cannot — somebody always notices.

listenings.text: Two things about recap emails, and they are the two that people get wrong. The first is that a recap is not a transcript. Nobody wants to know what was said. They want to know what was decided, who is doing what, and by when. If your email is longer than the meeting felt, you have written the wrong thing. The second one matters more. When you report what somebody else said, be careful with the verb you choose, because the verb is your judgement and everybody reads it as one. He said he would look at it is not the same as he agreed to deliver it, and he promised is not the same as he mentioned. I have seen a working relationship damaged by one word in a summary, where the meeting itself had been perfectly friendly. So report what was said, choose the verb that matches what was actually meant, and if you are not sure which verb that is, use said.

I write the recap in the same shape every single time, and it takes me about eight minutes. First line: what the meeting was about, in one sentence. Then, decisions. Not discussion, decisions. Then the actions, and every action has a name and a date, because an action without a name is a wish. Then anything that is still open, with the name of the person it is waiting for. And the last line is what I want them to remember if they read nothing else. When I report what somebody said, I keep it short and I keep it neutral. She said the invoice would arrive on Friday. He asked whether the forecast had been updated. They agreed to review it before the close. Three shapes, and they cover almost everything I ever need to write.
